whoIsThisFor.heading: Who should take the Tableau Architect exam?

personas.label: Enterprise architects
personas.description: You plan how Tableau is deployed, secured, and scaled across a large organization.

personas.label: Tableau Server administrators
personas.description: You operate Tableau today and want to take responsibility for its architecture.

personas.label: Analytics platform leaders
personas.description: You oversee business-wide analytics, including governance and platform costs.

examDifficulty.heading: How challenging is the Tableau Architect exam?
examDifficulty.summary: This exam focuses on operating Tableau at scale rather than creating individual views. It covers deployment design and capacity, governed data sources, row-level security, and performance as usage grows.
bullets: 54 scored questions in 105 minutes, plus up to five unscored questions that do not count.
63% to pass, which is 35 correct answers out of 54.
Platform architecture. Review processes, topology, sizing, high availability, and upgrades.
Governance. Study projects, permissions, trusted data sources, and content lifecycle.
examDifficulty.passRateGuidance: Practise sizing a deployment for a given user population, matching process capacity to a performance issue, and applying row-level security without workbook duplication. Aim for at least 75% on practice questions.

examFormat.heading: Tableau Architect exam format
examFormat.intro: You can sit the proctored exam online or at a test centre. Questions often describe an organizational need and ask for the right platform design.
examFormat.scenarioPercent: Scenarios may describe slow month-end dashboards, the need to keep regional data separate, or another operational constraint. Choose the design or setting that addresses the stated need.
bestWayToPass: Know each server process: Understand VizQL, backgrounder, data engine, repository, and gateway, and identify which process matches a symptom.
Centralize row-level security: A published data source with user-based entitlements can support many audiences in one workbook.
Compare Cloud and Server: Understand how managed hosting changes control, upgrades, and operating costs.
Plan governance: Organize projects, set group permissions, certify trusted sources, and retire unused content.

certificationCard.description: This exam covers architecture for Tableau at scale: deployment, capacity, governed data sources, row-level security, performance, and content lifecycle. The exam is 54 scored questions in 105 minutes, with a 63% pass mark, weighted towards Monitor and Maintain a Tableau Deployment (41%) and Deploy Tableau Server (37%).

blocks.heading: Deployment topology and processes
blocks.body: Tableau Server processes have different roles. The gateway routes incoming requests. VizQL renders views, so it is relevant when many users experience slow interactive dashboards. Backgrounder runs extract refreshes and subscriptions, so queued refreshes point to its capacity. The data engine stores and queries extracts. The repository is a PostgreSQL database for platform metadata, users, permissions, and usage history. Tableau Cloud removes server infrastructure management but provides less control over topology and upgrade timing.

blocks.heading: Governed data sources
blocks.body: At scale, publish and govern the data source rather than defining data separately in each workbook. Shared joins, calculations, and names help teams report consistent measures. Certification signals that a source is trusted. Choose live connections when up-to-date data is required and the source can handle queries; choose extracts when speed or reduced source load matters and scheduled freshness is sufficient. Set refresh timing to match the business need.

blocks.heading: Permissions and row-level security
blocks.body: Content permissions control who can view or edit workbooks and data sources. Manage them through groups and projects where possible. Row-level security controls which records appear to a user and can let one workbook serve multiple audiences. A common pattern uses an entitlements table that maps users to permitted records, then applies a logged-in-user filter on the published data source so dependent workbooks inherit it. Duplicating workbooks for each region increases maintenance and risks inconsistency.

blocks.heading: Performance and scale
blocks.body: First simplify the content and queries before adding hardware. Reduce extracts by filtering rows, removing unused fields, or aggregating data. Keep dashboards focused because sheets and quick filters add queries. Review wide crosstabs and calculations that force row-level work over large tables. Then add capacity that matches the bottleneck: VizQL for interactive rendering or backgrounder for refresh queues. High availability uses redundant processes across nodes so one failure does not stop the service.

blocks.heading: Governance and content lifecycle
blocks.body: Organize projects around the business and use group permissions so new content inherits appropriate access. Decide who may publish and who may view. Certify trusted data sources and distinguish them from experiments. Use repository usage data to find content that is no longer used and retire it. Agree on naming conventions and monitor licence use so the platform remains manageable and its costs visible.

scenarioTips.h2: How to prepare for the Tableau Architect exam
scenarioTips.intro: Identify the symptom or constraint in each scenario, then choose the platform process, setting, or governance control that directly addresses it.

blocks.heading: Match capacity to the bottleneck
blocks.body: Slow interactive views point to VizQL. Delayed or queued extract refreshes point to backgrounder capacity.

blocks.heading: Design reusable row-level security
blocks.body: Use user entitlements on the published data source so one governed workbook can serve different audiences.

blocks.heading: Compare hosting choices
blocks.body: Cloud removes infrastructure operations but limits control of upgrades and topology. Self-managed Server offers more control and more operational work.

blocks.heading: Design for availability
blocks.body: Run redundant key processes across multiple nodes so one failure does not stop the platform.

blocks.heading: Manage content over time
blocks.body: Use repository activity to identify unused dashboards and remove stale content that consumes resources and reduces trust.

nextCertsAfter.intro: Build on your Tableau architecture knowledge with these related Salesforce credentials:

sampleQuestions.question: Extract refreshes are queued and finish hours late, but interactive dashboards are responsive. Which capacity should be increased?
sampleQuestions.explanation: Backgrounder processes extract refreshes and subscriptions, so its capacity is relevant to a refresh queue.
whyWrong: VizQL renders views, which are already responsive.
The gateway routes requests and is not the bottleneck described.
The repository stores metadata; it does not run the refresh jobs.

sampleQuestions.question: Regional managers should see only their own rows while the organization maintains one dashboard. What should the architect implement?
options: A separate Tableau site for each region
Use row-level security with user entitlements
A separate workbook for each region
A quick filter users set to their region
sampleQuestions.explanation: Row-level security can filter data for each logged-in user while allowing the same dashboard to serve multiple regions.
whyWrong: Separate sites add operational overhead for a row-level requirement.
Duplicated workbooks increase maintenance and can drift apart.
A user-controlled quick filter is not a security control.

sampleQuestions.question: At month end, hundreds of users open dashboards and interactive views slow down, while refreshes finish on time. What should be scaled?
sampleQuestions.explanation: VizQL renders views for interactive users, so a concurrency problem during viewing points to VizQL capacity.
whyWrong: Backgrounder runs refreshes, which are completing on time.
More extract storage does not address interactive rendering.
Projects organize content and do not provide rendering capacity.

sampleQuestions.question: A company wants to avoid server maintenance, patching, and upgrade planning. Which option fits, and what does it give up?
options: Self-managed Server, with no operational trade-off
sampleQuestions.explanation: Tableau Cloud removes server operations but gives the provider more control over infrastructure and upgrade timing.
whyWrong: Desktop is an authoring client, not a hosted sharing platform.
Self-managed Server requires the maintenance the company wants to avoid.
Prep supports data preparation, not hosting dashboards.

sampleQuestions.question: Different teams report different values for the same business measure. What is a strong architectural response?
options: Train each team to write calculations independently
Hold a monthly meeting to reconcile reports
sampleQuestions.explanation: A governed, certified source gives teams a shared definition and reduces conflicting calculations.
whyWrong: Licenses do not standardize measure definitions.
Training does not prevent separate definitions from drifting later.
Reconciliation treats each month’s symptom rather than standardizing the source.

sampleQuestions.question: Which Tableau Server component stores users, permissions, metadata, and usage history?
sampleQuestions.explanation: The repository is the PostgreSQL database that stores Tableau Server metadata and usage information.
whyWrong: VizQL renders visualizations.
The gateway routes incoming requests.
The data engine stores and queries extracts.

sampleQuestions.question: Extract refreshes are slow. What should the team try before adding platform hardware?
options: Change every workbook to a live connection
sampleQuestions.explanation: Reducing unnecessary data and fields can make extracts more efficient before the platform is scaled.
whyWrong: More frequent runs of a slow extract may worsen the queue.
Optimize the extract before adding capacity.
Live connections can shift more load to the source database.

sampleQuestions.question: How should access permissions be managed in a large Tableau deployment?
options: Grant permissions to groups at the project level
Set permissions for each person on every workbook
Export PDFs for people who lack access
sampleQuestions.explanation: Group permissions at the project level scale better and can provide sensible defaults for new content.
whyWrong: Per-user, per-workbook permission management becomes difficult to maintain.
Shared accounts reduce accountability.
PDFs can bypass access controls and become outdated.

sampleQuestions.question: What does certifying a data source communicate?
options: That only administrators can use it
sampleQuestions.explanation: Certification signals that users can rely on a data source as an approved source.
whyWrong: Certification does not change refresh speed.
Certification is not an encryption setting.
Certified sources are intended to be used by appropriate users, not administrators alone.

sampleQuestions.question: How can an architect identify dashboards that are no longer used?
options: Delete all content more than one year old
sampleQuestions.explanation: Repository usage information helps identify content with little or no recent activity.
whyWrong: File size does not show whether content is used.
Surveys may miss actual usage and take time to collect.
Age alone does not show whether a dashboard is valuable.

sampleQuestions.question: What supports high availability in a Tableau Server deployment?
options: Take a daily repository backup only
sampleQuestions.explanation: Redundancy across nodes helps the platform continue when a process or node fails.
whyWrong: Extracts are unrelated to high availability.
Backups aid recovery but do not provide continued operation.
One server is still a single point of failure.

sampleQuestions.question: The warehouse changes only once each night, but live queries create heavy load whenever users open dashboards. What should change?
options: Buy a larger warehouse instance first
Ask users to open dashboards less often
sampleQuestions.explanation: A scheduled extract provides data refreshed nightly while reducing repeated queries to the warehouse.
whyWrong: A larger warehouse may be unnecessary if nightly freshness is sufficient.
VizQL capacity does not reduce the number of source queries.
Restricting dashboard use does not meet the business need.

sampleQuestions.question: What is a major risk of building separate workbooks for each audience instead of using row-level security?
options: Copies need updates and can drift
sampleQuestions.explanation: Duplicated workbooks require repeated changes and can drift into different versions.
whyWrong: Rendering speed is not the primary drawback.
Each workbook still needs appropriate permissions.
More workbooks increase maintenance and refresh work.

sampleQuestions.question: What should the Tableau project structure generally reflect?
options: The way the business is organized
The date each dashboard was created
The file size of the workbooks
The alphabetical order of workbook titles
sampleQuestions.explanation: Projects aligned to business areas make it easier to manage group access and content.
whyWrong: Creation date does not show who should use the content.
Workbook size is not an organizational structure.
Alphabetical names do not express business ownership or access.

sampleQuestions.question: A dashboard has twelve worksheets and nine quick filters and is slow. What is a likely contributor?
options: Worksheets and filters each add queries
The server is running low on disk space
sampleQuestions.explanation: Many worksheets and filters can trigger many queries, making the dashboard slower.
whyWrong: Row-level security is not automatically enabled and is not the stated cause.
Certification is a governance label and does not affect query performance.
Disk capacity is not the most likely explanation for this dashboard design.
